title: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning
author: Gabe Pereyra · Nico

kp.k: Legal agent benchmarking models associate work and partner evaluation
kp.d: Pereyra describes Harvey’s open-sourced Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) as a move beyond its earlier chat-based BigLaw Bench. By analogy with coding benchmarks, LAB combines matter documents, high-level partner requests and legal unit tests reflecting how partners or senior associates assess work. His diligence example tests whether an agent identifies consequential change-of-control provisions and produces a diligence memo. He argues that substantial BigLaw work is quantifiable, while acknowledging that extending this approach across practice areas requires task-specific evaluation design.
qs: before legal agent bench, we had big law bench, which was more of a chat-based benchmark
And I think there's a bit of a misconception that, "Oh, legal's subjective, so you can't do this."

a lot of what we're building is essentially this taxonomy of here's all the tasks that a law firm would do and here's all the subtasks that associates would do and how partners or senior associates would grade that work.

kp.k: Synthetic benchmark data combines agents with lawyer review
kp.d: Nico says confidentiality prevented freely sharing firm documents for an open-source benchmark. Harvey instead used agents to draft synthetic material, guided by its applied legal research team of former BigLaw attorneys. The team mapped 24 practice areas and their tasks, document types and realistic deal characteristics; a larger lawyer group reviewed outputs, rubrics and document quality. This is a reported dataset-construction method, not evidence that unreviewed synthetic documents meet lawyer standards.
qs: the way that we did it was actually agent-led with lawyer review.
Obviously not good enough to be lawyer passing.
We basically mapped out 24 practice areas that law firms have on their websites
it ends up being a pretty like human-in-the-loop but scalable way to generate data.

kp.k: Model selection increasingly balances quality, cost and latency
kp.d: Both speakers argue that aggregate benchmark rankings are insufficient for production decisions because models differ by task, price and speed. Pereyra reports strong Anthropic performance but areas where “5.5” or open-source models do better; he later describes Opus 4.7 as three times more expensive than 5.5 for 10 or 20% greater performance. Nico identifies Opus 47 as the current leader and describes Gemini 3.5 Flash as approximately seven times faster than some frontier models. These are speakers’ initial benchmark comparisons; the transcript supplies no score table or detailed measurement conditions.
qs: every different model is good at something different.
it's which model can solve the task at the lowest price point
Opus 4.7 is three times more expensive than 5.5, but it's, you know, 10 or 20% more performant.
Or like Gemini 3.5 Flash, it's like seven times faster at completing work than some of the frontier, uh, models.

kp.k: Harvey positions organizational infrastructure above general legal intelligence
kp.d: Pereyra distinguishes Harvey’s intended organizational productivity role for firms and large in-house departments from the individual productivity products he attributes to model laboratories. His strategy is to open-source general legal capabilities while building infrastructure through which clients can own models and systems using sensitive, unique data. He compares this competitive relationship with model providers to companies that build on cloud platforms while also competing with them.
qs: the products we're trying to build are organizational productivity for law firms or large in-house departments.
we don't see the general legal intelligence as where the value of kind of Harvey comes from.
we want to open source the general stuff and work with all of the providers to make these models as good as possible at general legal.
we want to build infrastructure for these law firms and enterprises that help them own their own models and build their own systems on their unique data.

kp.k: Client confidentiality and platform risk motivate multiple model providers
kp.d: Pereyra argues that firms need multiple model providers to accommodate clients’ sensitivities and avoid dependence on one provider’s compute availability or capabilities. His hypothetical example is a firm representing OpenAI being unable to send its sensitive legal data to Anthropic. Separately, he describes Harvey’s shared spaces product as enabling firm–client collaboration and identifies relationship-specific model training as an unresolved development objective subject to ethical, regulatory and client-data obligations, rather than an established permission to pool client data.
qs: Open AI is not going to let you send their sensitive legal data to Anthropic's models.
Like what happens if you pick one provider and they run out of compute, their models fall behind.
At a law firm, a lot of the data is all of their clients, and you can't mix this.
how can we help law firms use their data in a way that respects kind of all of their client obligations, but still be able to improve their systems based on that?

kp.k: Agentic workflows increase capability, adoption and operating costs
kp.d: Pereyra reports a transition over the preceding 6 months from a chat-based lawyer copilot toward cloud-hosted agents using tools and sandboxes. He says models now generate entire documents and are beginning to be useful enough for lawyers to change established routines. Longer runs, higher token use and increased adoption jointly raise costs: he gives examples of a single document-drafting query costing $20 and reviews involving up to 100,000 uploaded contracts costing $20,000. These are vendor-reported examples, not average costs or demonstrated autonomous legal-service outcomes.
qs: the original product we built was kind of this chat-based co-pilot for lawyers
now you need sandboxes. The models use way more tokens.
a single query can cost $20.
you can upload 100,000 contracts and ask the models to review them and some of those can cost $20,000.
they're using more tokens because they're running for longer and they work so much better that users are using them more.

kp.k: Cost pressures favor routing and specialized open-source models
kp.d: Pereyra says Harvey was previously capability-constrained and therefore favored the largest models, but growing usage has made serving costs a central concern over the past 6 months. The host cites Winston’s 13 trillion token figure, which Pereyra acknowledges without supplying a measurement period. His proposed responses include benchmark-informed routing, shifting traffic to open-source models and post-training narrower models for tasks such as diligence. Achieving frontier-level task performance without frontier-level cost is presented as an opportunity, not a completed result.
qs: I think Winston mentioned you guys got up to 13 trillion.
up until recently we've always been capability constrained.
not every task needs to be sent to the largest models.
I probably don't need a trillion parameters if I just need the system to be good at diligence.
how do you build products and models in a way that you can get that frontier performance without kind of all of the frontier cost.

kp.k: AI pricing inherits legal work’s measurement and negotiation problems
kp.d: Pereyra challenges expectations that consumption pricing or pricing completed work will straightforwardly solve AI monetization. He compares work-based pricing with firms’ fixed-fee difficulties and defends hourly billing as a scalable way to price heterogeneous, complex work. He reports firms saying that negotiating bespoke prices across 10,000 clients is impractical. He describes Harvey’s evolution from an enterprise subscription business toward consumption while retaining both approaches, and speculates that forecasting difficulties could eventually bring pricing back toward subscriptions.
qs: buying off tokens is insanely complicated.
it'll probably at some point go back to something like subscription cuz it's hard to like forecast these things.
the problem you run into of pricing the work is actually the same problem that law firms run into when they try to do fixed fee pricing
it lets you price incredibly complex work at massive scale in a way that the entire industry can agree on.
we just have a 10,000 clients. We can't negotiate every engagement and price this, and everyone's different.

kp.k: Token bills may require detailed accounting and competitive discipline
kp.d: Pereyra predicts that large consumption bills will prompt demands for explanations of agent activity analogous to clients demanding six-minute billing records from law firms. His $10 million consumption bill is hypothetical, not a reported Harvey customer bill. He argues that consumption creates incentives for model providers to increase token use, creating demand for benchmarking, routing and cost-optimization services. However, he qualifies the incentive critique by arguing that competition among model providers, including open-source alternatives, can constrain prices, just as he believes competition disciplines law-firm hourly billing.
qs: all these customers are going to start getting these consumption bills of like $10 million
tell me what every associate did for every 6-minute increment on the entire project
I think you're going to start seeing things like this for token billing
they're somewhat incentivized to have their agents use as many tokens as possible.
if open source catches up, you're also going to have pricing pressure.

kp.k: Domain-specific agent infrastructure becomes a research priority
kp.d: Nico describes the agent harness as the tools, skills and delegation infrastructure surrounding a model, including document reading and writing, web search and coding. He reports that specialization and legal expertise matter and proposes collaborative development by lawyers, researchers and the open-source community. He also reports early indications that post-trained open-weight models narrow the gap with closed-source frontier models. Pereyra similarly sees reasoning-time compute, reinforcement-learning environments and improved infrastructure expanding opportunities for application-layer companies.
qs: the harness is basically the way that you define all of these tools, skills, how agents can delegate to to to other agents to to complete tasks.
specialization matters and domain expertise matters
we're starting to see early results that show that open-weight models, when post-trained, kind of close the gap with with the closed-source frontier.
the more that kind of shifts the ability to application layer companies to do interesting things.

kp.k: Organizational human–agent collaboration remains a conditional next frontier
kp.d: Nico predicts LAB will become saturated within a year and that the episode’s year will bring a shift from individual intelligence toward organizational intelligence. For Harvey, he frames this as supporting lawyer–lawyer collaboration and human–agent teams, rather than merely improving base models. He explicitly conditions this research agenda on models becoming sufficiently capable, saying inadequate model performance has previously prevented exploration. The transcript does not establish resulting changes to staffing, junior hiring or partnership structures.
qs: I do think the benchmark gets saturated within a year at least.
this year is the year that we see intelligence at an individual level kind of brought into intelligence at an organizational level
How do human agent teams collaborate?
we haven't been able to explore yet because the models are not good enough
if we make the models good enough, then we can do really innovative research in my opinion.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pereyra and Nico describe a shift from individual legal copilots toward task-performing agents and organizational collaboration, with model selection, confidential-data infrastructure and rising consumption costs becoming central.
pts.d: Gabe Pereyra claims that much BigLaw work can be quantified using task-specific criteria analogous to software unit tests. Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), distinct from its earlier chat-based BigLaw Bench, represents legal assignments through documents, partner instructions and criteria for assessing associate-style work products. He describes recent improvements enabling entire-document generation and encouraging lawyers to change established routines. However, he also says that, until recently, even leading models were insufficient for benchmark tasks; he does not establish comprehensive autonomous legal capability. He argues that different models suit different tasks and that sufficiently capable, cheaper models should handle simpler work. He predicts opportunities for specialized models that deliver frontier-level performance on a narrow legal task without the full cost of a general-purpose frontier model. He positions Harvey's value as organizational infrastructure rather than general legal intelligence: supporting multiple providers, insulating firms from provider and client-confidentiality risks, and helping firms and corporate legal departments build systems on their own sensitive data. Shared workspaces between firms and clients are presented as a possible basis for relationship-specific models, subject to client obligations. Pereyra also claims that longer-running agents, improving usefulness and increased adoption are jointly driving sharply higher token consumption and costs. He predicts that consumption pricing will create difficult-to-explain bills and demand for detailed usage accounting, benchmarking and routing. He challenges the assumption that AI straightforwardly replaces hourly legal billing with fixed fees: fixed pricing requires engagement-specific negotiation, whereas hourly billing supplies an industry-wide mechanism for pricing complex work. He suggests AI subscriptions may eventually reappear because token spending is hard to forecast, and argues competition among model and inference providers should constrain pricing incentives. Nico claims that specialized legal tools and agent infrastructure improve performance, and that post-trained open-weight models are beginning to narrow the gap with closed frontier models. He predicts LAB saturation within a year and a transition toward collaboration among lawyers and human-agent teams at the organizational level.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of Harvey's own benchmark, internal product and usage experience, and customer discussions; future market and organizational outcomes are forecasts.
pts.d: For the quantifiability claim, Pereyra gives a diligence example: an agent receives a contract data room and high-level partner request, produces a diligence memo, and is assessed on findings such as material change-of-control provisions. Nico explains that LAB uses synthetic documents initially generated by agents, guided by former BigLaw lawyers across 24 mapped practice areas, with lawyer review of outputs, rubrics and document quality. This is a vendor-created benchmark intended to mirror legal work, not a reported evaluation on freely shared confidential client files. Their reported initial results support task-dependent quality, cost and speed comparisons: Pereyra says Anthropic is strong overall but other models lead in some areas; he describes Opus 4.7 as three times the cost of 5.5 for 10–20% more performance. Nico identifies Opus 47 as the current leader and says Gemini 3.5 Flash completes work about seven times faster than some frontier models. These figures are attributed to the speakers; the transcript supplies no underlying tables, scoring denominators or detailed comparison protocols. For rising costs, Pereyra reports that a document-drafting query can cost $20 and that some reviews involving an upload capacity of 100,000 contracts can cost $20,000. He also invokes internal usage plots and customer adoption, without quantified longitudinal data. The 13-trillion-token figure is introduced by the interviewer and receives a brief assent, rather than a separately specified measurement by Pereyra. His argument about fixed-fee difficulty draws on conversations with law firms, while future token-billing scrutiny and competitive pricing pressure rely on analogy with professional-services billing. His example of a firm representing OpenAI while using Anthropic models is hypothetical, illustrating his claimed confidentiality/provider-conflict risk rather than a documented incident. Nico describes early post-training results and repeated experience with specialization but gives no numerical improvement estimates. Benchmark saturation, organizational transformation and eventual pricing arrangements remain predictions, not demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source locates the legal-agent inflection in the preceding six months, reports newly released benchmark results, and forecasts benchmark saturation and organizational progress over approximately the following year.
pts.d: The document dates the interview to 2026 but gives no exact recording date. Pereyra repeatedly places Harvey's transition from a chat copilot toward cloud-based agents, improved legal usefulness and rising consumption in the preceding six months. Nico says LAB launched about two weeks before his interview and initial closed-frontier-model results were posted that day. His expectation of benchmark saturation is phrased as 'within a year at least'; his organizational-collaboration prediction concerns 'this year.' Neither should be converted into a precise calendar deadline. Pereyra's broad cost escalation forecast is conditional on more users adopting long-horizon agents as intensively as current power users. Cheaper routing depends on smaller or open models being sufficiently capable for the task, not universally substitutable for frontier models. His suggested specialized-model economics are a development opportunity rather than an accomplished result. Proprietary model training is explicitly contingent on ethical, regulatory and client-data constraints; the speakers do not claim that client information can simply be pooled. Multi-provider infrastructure is justified by client sensitivities, potential compute shortages and provider performance changes. Nico qualifies aggregate benchmark scores by cost, latency and practice-area differences. His organizational vision requires models first becoming good enough to support higher-level collaboration. Predictions about subscriptions, token-accounting ecosystems and competition have no fixed dates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern large law firms, their corporate clients, large in-house legal departments and the AI providers serving them, rather than individual consumers or unmet civil legal need.
pts.d: Large law firms are expected to integrate agents into substantive work across practice areas, select models according to quality and economics, accommodate different clients' provider restrictions, and manage potentially volatile consumption bills. Associates' diligence and other assignments provide the template for agent tasks; partners' and senior associates' assessment criteria provide the template for benchmark scoring. This does not amount to a stated prediction of associate job losses, altered staffing leverage or elimination of human checking. Lawyers are described as beginning to adopt tools when their usefulness outweighs the disruption of changing routines, with future collaboration extending to human-agent teams. Corporate clients, including a hypothetical private-equity client, may collaborate with outside counsel in shared workspaces and potentially benefit from systems adapted to their relationship-specific data, subject to confidentiality and other obligations. Large corporate legal departments are explicitly part of Harvey's organizational-productivity market. Harvey, a software provider, is positioned as a multi-model infrastructure and optimization layer, while frontier labs face competition from one another and from open models. Inference providers are expected to benefit from demand for lower-cost serving and privately controlled models. Buyers of AI services may need granular explanations of agent spending analogous to detailed legal invoices. The transcript makes no concrete access-to-justice, ALSP market-share or legal employment forecast.
